stem: A research lab still has 30 IAM users that developers use for console and AWS CLI work. The CISO requires that API calls be made only after MFA and wants to stop issuing long-lived access keys to people. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Update the IAM account password policy so that it requires an MFA code at every console sign-in and CLI call
Rotate every developer's access keys every 90 days by using a scheduled Lambda function
Attach a policy that denies all actions except MFA setup when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false
Enable MFA on the root user only, because IAM users inherit the root user's MFA device
Move developers to IAM Identity Center so that the CLI gets temporary credentials instead of access keys

rationale: A policy with a Deny statement that uses BoolIfExists on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to false blocks every action except the MFA setup actions until the user has authenticated with MFA; CLI users then call sts:GetSessionToken with their MFA code. IAM Identity Center gives human users temporary credentials for the console and CLI and has its own MFA settings, which removes the need for long-lived access keys. The IAM account password policy controls password length, complexity, expiration and reuse; it has no MFA option and does not apply to access keys. Rotating access keys still issues long-lived keys to people, which is what the CISO wants to stop. MFA is registered per identity; each user needs their own device, and the root user's MFA does nothing for IAM users.
